pages.text: The countdown on the classroom wall said six days to the mock exams. Vivian stared at it. Her notes were in a pile, her textbooks were still wrapped in her bag, and her plan was, well, to panic. “I will start tomorrow,” she told herself, for the fifth night in a row. Her friend Reuben raised an eyebrow. “Tomorrow is a very busy day,” he said. “It has not arrived yet.”

“It has not arrived yet.”
pages.alt: A girl stares at a wall calendar with a countdown while a pile of untouched notes sits on her desk.

pages.text: Mr Ampadu wrote a timetable on the board. “Revision is a skill, and skills can be learned,” he said. “First, list the subjects. Second, decide which are your weakest. Third, give each one a time slot. Fourth, take breaks.” He turned and smiled. “And please do not study all night. The brain needs sleep to remember what it has learned.”

pages.text: Vivian, Reuben and Mercy formed a study group. They met after school for forty minutes each day. Reuben made flash cards for Integrated Science. Mercy drew mind maps for Social Studies. Vivian practised past questions in English. “We test each other,” said Mercy. “If you can explain it to a friend, you really understand it.”

pages.text: On Wednesday, Vivian’s phone buzzed for the tenth time. A group chat was arguing about football. She switched it off and put it in her bag. “Phone away, notes out,” she told herself. Mercy nodded. “Our brains are like a muscle,” she said. “If we split our attention in ten pieces, none of them gets stronger.”

pages.text: On Sunday night, the night before the mock, Vivian did not cram. She read her summary notes for an hour, packed her bag with pens, a ruler, a calculator and her examination number, and went to bed at nine. “Sleep is part of revision,” she said sleepily. “Mr Ampadu said so.”

pages.text: On Monday, the English paper began. Vivian read each question twice, planned her essay in the margin, watched the clock and left five minutes at the end to check her spelling. When the bell rang, she put down her pen with a calm heart. “I did not know everything,” she told Reuben. “But I know I gave it my best.”

pages.alt: A girl sits at an exam desk, writing carefully with a clock on the wall.

pages.text: That weekend, Vivian wrote to her young cousin Akos, who would take his own exams next year. “Dear Akos, I hope you are keeping well. I am writing to share some advice on preparing for exams. First, make a timetable and follow it. Second, study with friends who encourage you. Third, switch off your phone while you study. Finally, sleep well the night before. Good luck, and write soon. Your cousin, Vivian.”

pages.text: Exam-safe tip: Vivian’s letter gave clear advice using linking words such as first, second and finally, which help a marker follow the order of ideas. She wrote “Good luck” and not “GL” or “gud luk”. Her advice came with reasons, because a letter is stronger when it explains why. The end.
